evidence: Cic. Fam. 4.14.1: mē meam prīstinam dignitātem obtinēre
terms.comment: The standing a man has from office and conduct, and the respect it commands (Lewis & Short); the thing a Roman politician would least give up. It also means worthiness, and of persons and things, dignity, grandeur.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 4.4.1: ex prīstinō statū nostrō
terms.comment: One’s condition and place in society (Lewis & Short): free or slave, citizen or not, high or low; Traupman’s dē statū mulierum, on the status of women. First of all a way of standing, a posture; for the state things are in, see state (condition).
Of birth and rank: summō locō nātus, of the highest birth; humilī locō, of low birth (Caes. BG 7.39).

phrases.latin: ego autem, sī dignitās est bene dē rē pūblicā sentīre et bonīs virīs probāre quod sentiās, obtineō dignitātem meam
phrases.english: but if standing means thinking rightly about the state and having good men approve what you think, I keep my standing

phrases.latin: nōn ut aliquid ex prīstinō statū nostrō retineāmus, sed ut quam honestissimē lūgeāmus
phrases.english: not to keep anything of our former position, but to mourn as honourably as we can

sources: Lewis & Short: dignitas · Lewis & Short: status · Lewis & Short: locus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 25, 385.
Cicero, Letters to Friends 4.4 and 4.14, and Caesar, Gallic War 5.25 and 7.39, checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
